newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: President Aleman's "honeymoon" starts in Nicaragua.
newsitem.headline: President Aleman's "honeymoon" starts in Nicaragua.

text.p: Nicaraguan President Arnoldo Aleman has sailed through his first weeks in office, confounding predictions of a troubled start to his presidency by making peace with even his most bitter political enemies.

The right-wing Aleman took office on Jan. 10 amid fears of social unrest by his rival left-wing Sandinistas, a nasty power struggle in the National Assembly and continued attacks by armed bands left over from civil war in the countryside.
Nicaraguans remember a rocky start for his predecessor, Violeta Chamorro, when general strikes by Sandinista unions, economic chaos and fears of an army coup held the fledgling government hostage.
But in dizzying two weeks, Aleman has met with almost all of Nicaragua's squabbling factions, largely putting out the fires of a feared social conflict.

"Things have started very well for Aleman. People clearly want to give this government a chance," Adolfo Calero, a former right-wing Contra rebel leader who is now a conservative congressman, told Reuters.

Three days after Aleman took office, former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega, who had complained bitterly about election fraud by Aleman's party, went to Aleman's office to negotiate Nicaragua's political stability.

They agreed to try to negotiate a resolution to the problem of private property confiscated by the state during the 1979-1990 Sandinista government, a major roadblock in the road to a reconciliation between Nicaragua's right and left wings.
Ortega's turnaround surprised even Aleman, a 51-year-old former lawyer and mayor of Managua.
"Commander Ortega has undergone a total transformation that has surprised me. He has shown an openness and willingness to resolve the property problem," Aleman told reporters.
Days later, gun-toting leaders of armed gangs left over from its civil war, which ended in 1990, began assembling in specially designated "peace zones" to begin peace talks with the new government.

Then, two weeks into his presidency, leaders of militant Sandinista unions, famed for their vigorous street protests, met with Aleman, offering labour peace in exchange for guarantees their would be no mass firings of state employees.
Once fiery communist union leaders said while they had not discarded striking, their top priority was preserving the jobs of members of their depleted ranks, not starting a labour war.
"Politically he has acted very capably, and in practical terms the results of his reconciliation initiative have been good. But it is still early," political analyst Alejandro Serrano said.
Nicaragua's long-suffering business community triumphantly announced the arrival of political stability in Nicaragua and has rolled out the red carpet for foreign investment.
The only fly in the ointment, said Serrano, was the fight between Aleman's Liberals and the Sandinistas over the formation of commissions in the National Assembly.
